segments.title: 3. Using the sprite sheet (games + consoles)
lines: atlas.png = one row per move, one cell per frame.
atlas.json / sprites.cfg / character.ini say where each frame is, fps, loop, ground line.
A PROFILE writes the exact files an engine wants (Godot, Unity, Tiled, Phaser, ini...).
A CONSOLE target also writes palette + 8x8 tiles + a C header within that console's limits.

script.cap: Help > 'How to use a sprite sheet' explains the layout and the code to draw a frame
Help > 'Output profiles': one JSON file per kind of game - make your own with 'Create profile...'
Back to Build: a fighter from a photo (front = user photo, side/back = SYNTHETIC renders)
Profile fighter14: 14 fighting-game moves, atlas + sprites.cfg
Console target SNES: frames shrunk to 64px, 15 colours + transparent, 8x8 4bpp tiles, C header
Building the sheet, the views and the SNES export
Done - preview a move (kick). Moves other than idle are labelled placeholders made from the photo
The log shows the console result and the limits it checked
out/teal_hero/ has the standard files and console/ with the SNES data

items: console/: indexed sheet, palette, 8x8 tiles - tools/verify_console.py checks every limit (PASS)

segments.title: In a game
lines: A game adapter maps the sheet to the game's format.
Here: tools/export_ef.py -> Egyptian Fighter (one strip per move + its sprites.cfg).
Engines: load the profile's file - e.g. Godot: the .tres SpriteFrames, Unity: .unity.json.

segments.title: Limits (honest)
lines: Console exports are data + a C header; you still need that console's toolchain / engine.
Photo moves other than idle are placeholders unless you import frames or a video per move.
Profiles only describe FILES - game logic stays in your game.
Help > Videos lists these tutorials; Help > Troubleshooting covers common problems.
